definition: Done or acting too quickly, without enough care or thought.
example: A hasty glance at the map sent the hikers down the wrong trail.
nuance: Hasty criticizes speed that costs care, while quick or prompt can praise speed that does no harm.
prompt: A student finishes an hour-long math test in only ten minutes.
options: Her hasty answers left several careless errors on the test.
Her hasty answers came only after she checked each problem twice.
She turned in the test and walked out of the room in hasty.
Her hasty answers earned praise for being thoughtful and thorough.
reasons: Rushing through the problems led to avoidable mistakes, which is exactly what the word points to.
Checking every problem twice shows patience and care, the reverse of rushing.
The phrase needs the noun haste; an adjective cannot follow the word in this way.
The word carries criticism for a lack of care, so it cannot describe thorough, praised work.

practice.prompt: A family is deciding whether to buy a house they toured for five minutes.
options: The hasty house had a sunny yard and three large bedrooms.
Their hasty offer came only after they weighed every pro and con for a year.
Buying after one brief visit was a hasty decision they soon regretted.
After months of inspections and research, they made a hasty offer.
reasons: A building cannot act too fast; the word describes people or their actions, not features.
A year of weighing pros and cons is the opposite of deciding without enough thought.
Committing to a big purchase after a short look, then regretting it, shows too little thought.
Months of careful research describe a slow, deliberate process, not a rushed one.
